literal: Prince of Qinghe, Prince of Yangping, Prince of Henan, Prince of Hejian, Prince of Changle, Prince of Guangping, Prince of Jingzhao
idiomatic: The Princes of Qinghe, Yangping, Henan, Hejian, Changle, Guangping, and Jingzhao

literal: Emperor Daowu had ten sons.
idiomatic: Taizu, Emperor Daowu, fathered ten sons.

literal: Empress Xuanmu of the Liu clan bore Emperor Mingyuan; Lady He bore Prince Shao of Qinghe; the Great Lady bore Prince Xi of Yangping; Lady Wang bore Prince Yao of Henan.
idiomatic: Empress Xuanmu Liu bore Emperor Mingyuan; Lady He bore Prince Shao of Qinghe; the Great Lady bore Prince Xi of Yangping; Lady Wang bore Prince Yao of Henan.

literal: The mothers of Prince Xiu of Hejian and Prince Chuwén of Changle are not recorded.
idiomatic: The mothers of Princes Xiu of Hejian and Chuwén of Changle are missing from the record.

literal: Lady Duan bore Prince Lian of Guangping and Prince Li of Jingzhao.
idiomatic: Lady Duan bore Prince Lian of Guangping and Prince Li of Jingzhao.

literal: The mothers of the princes Hun and Cong are also not recorded; all died young and left no heirs.
idiomatic: Princes Hun and Cong likewise lack recorded mothers; each died young without issue.

literal: Prince Shao of Qinghe was enfeoffed in the sixth year of Tianxing.
idiomatic: Prince Shao of Qinghe received his fief in Tianxing year 6.

literal: Fierce, cruel, and treacherous, he would not heed instruction.
idiomatic: Violent and devious, he refused all teaching.

literal: He loved to roam the lanes, rob travelers, hack at and shoot dogs and pigs for sport.
idiomatic: He wandered the alleys robbing passersby and hacking or shooting dogs and swine for amusement.

literal: Taizu once grew furious and hung him head-down in a well, letting him out only when near death.
idiomatic: Taizu once hung him upside down in a well and pulled him out only on the edge of death.

literal: Emperor Mingyuan often rebuked him with righteous principle; they fell out, and Mingyuan always feared he would rebel.
idiomatic: Emperor Mingyuan repeatedly chastised him with moral duty; the two were estranged, and Mingyuan lived in fear of revolt.

literal: Shao's mother, Lady He, had been condemned; Taizu imprisoned her in the palace and meant to kill her.
idiomatic: Lady He, Shao's mother, had incurred guilt; Taizu shut her in the palace and prepared her execution.

literal: Night fell before the decision was made.
idiomatic: Dusk came before sentence could be carried out.

literal: Lady He secretly told Shao, "How will you save me?"
idiomatic: Lady He whispered to Shao, "What will you do to save me?"

literal: That night Shao, with several men of his guard and eunuchs, crossed the palace wall and broke the ban.
idiomatic: That night Shao and a handful of guards and palace eunuchs scaled the palace and violated the curfew.

literal: Attendants on either side cried, "Bandits!"
idiomatic: Those beside the throne shouted, "Assassins!"

literal: Taizu started up in alarm, could not find bow or blade, and died suddenly.
idiomatic: Taizu leapt up in terror, found neither bow nor sword, and collapsed dead.

literal: Next day the palace gates did not open until noon; Shao claimed an edict summoning the hundred officials to stand north of the western palace's Front Gate, and from between the door panels he asked the ministers, "I have a father and I have an elder brother—which will you follow?"
idiomatic: The gates stayed shut until noon; Shao proclaimed an edict calling officials to face north before the western palace's Front Gate, then spoke through the door crack: "I have a father and an elder brother—which do you choose?"

literal: From princes and dukes down all were stunned and pale; none answered.
idiomatic: Princes and ministers alike stood pale and speechless.

literal: After a long silence Duke of Nanping Changsun Song said, "We follow the prince."
idiomatic: At length Changsun Song, Duke of Nanping, said, "We follow Your Highness."

literal: The ministers then knew the imperial carriage had halted at dusk, but not how the sovereign had departed; only Duke of Yinping Yuan Lie wept and left.
idiomatic: They knew the emperor was dead but not the manner of his passing; only Yuan Lie, Duke of Yinping, wept and withdrew.

literal: Court and countryside seethed; every man nursed a separate design.
idiomatic: Inside and outside the capital turmoil spread; hearts turned every way.

literal: Marquis of Feiru He Hu raised beacon-fires north of Anyang city; old men of the Helan tribe all rushed to him, and other former followers led sons and nephews to gather kin, banding together here and there.
idiomatic: He Hu, Marquis of Feiru, lit signal fires north of Anyang; Helan clansmen flocked to him while other old followers mustered sons and kin in scattered bands.

literal: Hearing the mood unsettled, Shao issued cloth and silk to princes and officials—from several hundred bolts for the highest to ten for the lowest.
idiomatic: Shao, sensing unrest, distributed cloth and silk down the ranks of nobility and office, hundreds of bolts to the great and ten to the humble.

literal: Earlier, Emperor Mingyuan had been abroad; hearing of the coup he returned and hid in the hills, sending men by night to Marquis of Beixin An Tong, and the host answered from every side.
idiomatic: Mingyuan, away on campaign, turned back on news of the revolt, concealed himself in the mountains, and sent night messengers to An Tong, Marquis of Beixin; multitudes rallied to him.

literal: When Mingyuan reached the west of the city, guards seized Shao and presented him.
idiomatic: At the city's west wall Mingyuan's men seized Shao and brought him in.

literal: Shao and his mother were then granted death; a dozen eunuchs and palace women who had acted within as accomplices were executed, and those who had first laid hands on the imperial carriage were dismembered alive at the capital's southern avenue and eaten by the ministers.
idiomatic: Shao and his mother were put to death; a dozen inner eunuchs and palace women who had aided the plot were killed, and those who had first struck at the sovereign were quartered alive in the southern street and devoured by the court.

literal: Shao was then sixteen.
idiomatic: Shao was sixteen years old.

literal: His mother was younger sister to Empress Xianming—beautiful and radiant.
idiomatic: Shao's mother was Empress Xianming's younger sister, famed for her beauty.

literal: When Taizu first visited the Helan tribe he saw her and was pleased; he told Empress Xianming and asked to take her, but the empress said, "You must not—she is too beautiful to be good, and she already has a husband."
idiomatic: On Taizu's first visit to the Helan he desired her and asked Empress Xianming for her hand; the empress refused: "Do not take her—beauty so extreme breeds ill, and she is already wed."

literal: Taizu secretly had her husband killed and took her in; she bore Shao, and in the end brought forth great treason.
idiomatic: Taizu had her husband murdered in secret and married her; she bore Shao, and at last mothered rebellion.

literal: Prince Xi of Yangping was enfeoffed in the sixth year of Tianxing.
idiomatic: Prince Xi of Yangping received his fief in Tianxing year 6.

literal: Clever and accomplished, with refined conduct, he was admired and honored among the clan.
idiomatic: Quick-witted and cultivated, he won the clan's esteem.

literal: When Emperor Mingyuan drilled troops in the eastern commanderies he ordered Xi to inspect twelve armies; the formations pleased him greatly, and Mingyuan rewarded him richly.
idiomatic: Mingyuan, drilling in the east, had Xi review twelve commands; the display won high praise and lavish gifts.

literal: Later he campaigned against the western Yueqin and earned merit.
idiomatic: He later campaigned against the western Yueqin with distinction.

literal: In the sixth year of Taichang he died, aged twenty-three.
idiomatic: He died in Taichang year 6 at twenty-three.

literal: Emperor Mingyuan mourned without end and granted warm-bright secret vessels; funeral gifts were complete.
idiomatic: Mingyuan grieved long and bestowed warm-bright burial vessels and full funeral honors.

literal: Xi had seven sons.
idiomatic: Xi left seven sons.

literal: The eldest, Ta, inherited the title.
idiomatic: The eldest son Ta succeeded to the title.

literal: Eight feet tall, handsome in bearing, prudent and steady, his martial skill surpassed others.
idiomatic: He stood eight feet, comely and grave, with martial arts above the common run.

literal: Following Shizu against the Mountain Hu chieftain White Dragon in Xihe, he stormed the city, then broke the remnant band elsewhere and took several thousand heads.
idiomatic: With Shizu he attacked the Mountain Hu White Dragon in Xihe, stormed his stronghold, routed the survivors elsewhere, and took thousands of heads.

literal: His fief was changed to Prince of Linhuai and he was made General Who Pacifies the East.
idiomatic: He was re-enfeoffed Prince of Linhuai and appointed General Who Pacifies the East.

literal: Soon he was made Prince of Huainan, commissioner with staff, commander of all military affairs in Yu, Luo, and Henan, General Who Guards the South with opening-office equal-to-three-division, and garrisoned Hulao.
idiomatic: He was soon Prince of Huainan, bearer of the staff, commander of Yu, Luo, and Henan, General Who Guards the South with opening-office equal-to-three-division, stationed at Hulao.

literal: His renown was very great.
idiomatic: His fame stood very high.

literal: Later with Prince Ti of Wuchang he led Bingzhou troops to crush the Tujing rebel Hu Cao Puhun in Hexi and pacified them.
idiomatic: Later he and Prince Ti of Wuchang led Bingzhou forces against the Tujing rebel Cao Puhun in Hexi and subdued him.

literal: He was made commissioner with staff, Grand General of the Vanguard, commander of all armies, marched north against the Ruru, defeated them, and moved army stores to Bigan city.
idiomatic: Made bearer of the staff and Grand General of the Vanguard commanding all armies, he marched north against the Ruru, broke them, and shifted supplies to Bigan.

literal: When Liu Yilong of Song sent generals to raid the border, Ta followed the campaign at Xuan'e and defeated them.
idiomatic: When Liu Yilong's generals raided the frontier Ta joined the Xuan'e campaign and routed them.

literal: He was made commissioner with staff, commander of Yong and Qin, General Who Guards the West with opening-office equal-to-three-division, and regional inspector of Yong, garrisoning Chang'an.
idiomatic: He became bearer of the staff, commander of Yong and Qin, General Who Guards the West with opening-office equal-to-three-division, inspector of Yong, at Chang'an.

literal: He soothed Qin territory and won the hearts of Chinese and tribes alike.
idiomatic: He pacified Qin and won both Chinese and tribal peoples.

literal: When Yilong again raided the southern marches, Ta's prestige was long established and he was again made commander-in-chief at Hulao.
idiomatic: As Yilong struck the south again, Ta's standing brought him back as supreme commander at Hulao.

literal: In Gaozong's time he was made commissioner with staff, commander of Liang, General Who Guards the West, his honors unchanged.
idiomatic: Under Gaozong he held the staff as commander of Liang and General Who Guards the West with honors as before.

literal: Early in Gaozu's reign he entered court as Grand Master of the Central Capital, became attendant-in-ordinary, then General Who Pacifies the West, and was promoted to Minister over the Masses.
idiomatic: At Gaozu's accession he entered as Grand Master of the Central Capital, became attendant-in-ordinary, then General Who Pacifies the West, and rose to Minister over the Masses.

literal: He was granted a cushioned carriage and staff; at court he need not hurry.
idiomatic: He received the cushioned carriage and staff and was excused from hurrying at audience.

literal: In the twelfth year of Taihe he died, aged seventy-three.
idiomatic: He died in Taihe year 12 at seventy-three.

literal: Gaozu was then occupied with the ancestral temple at the first offering; hearing of the death he suspended the rite.
idiomatic: Gaozu was at the first temple offering when news came; he canceled the ceremony.

literal: The imperial carriage came in person; he mourned bitterly and ordered officials to oversee the funeral with added ritual gifts.
idiomatic: The emperor came in person, grieved openly, and ordered supervised obsequies with extra gifts.

literal: Posthumously he was made General Who Pacifies the East and governor of Dingzhou; Minister over the Masses was unchanged.
idiomatic: He was posthumously General Who Pacifies the East and governor of Dingzhou, still Minister over the Masses.

literal: His posthumous name was Prince Jing.
idiomatic: His temple name was Prince Jing.

literal: Ta had three sons.
idiomatic: Ta had three sons.

literal: The heir Tuwán died young and was posthumously made Champion General, regional inspector of Bingzhou, and Marquis Shun of Jinyang.
idiomatic: Heir Tuwán died young and was posthumously Champion General, inspector of Bingzhou, Marquis Shun of Jinyang.

literal: His son Xian inherited the grandfather's title.
idiomatic: Son Xian succeeded to the grandfather's rank.

literal: He died; his posthumous name was Prince Xi.
idiomatic: On his death he was Prince Xi.

literal: His son Shizun inherited.
idiomatic: Son Shizun succeeded.

literal: In Emperor Shizong's time he was made General of the Vanguard, acting governor of Youzhou, and also acting commander of the Western Palace Guard; later he acted as governor of Qingzhou.
idiomatic: Under Shizong he became General of the Vanguard, acting governor of Youzhou and Western Palace Guard commander, then acting governor of Qingzhou.

literal: He was soon promoted to General of Valiant Cavalry.
idiomatic: He was soon made General of Valiant Cavalry.

literal: He went out as General Who Subdues the Barbarians and regional inspector of Youzhou.
idiomatic: He left court as General Who Subdues the Barbarians and inspector of Youzhou.

literal: Shizun was mild and sincere, winning people by honest guidance; the common folk delighted in him.
idiomatic: Shizun was gentle and open-hearted; the people took joy in his rule.

literal: In Suzong's time he was made regional inspector of Jingzhou with his former general's title.
idiomatic: Under Suzong he became inspector of Jingzhou at his existing rank.

literal: He was soon given the additional title General of the Front.
idiomatic: He soon received the added rank General of the Front.

literal: At first in Hanyang his reputation stood firm; later he took bribes and squandered frontier stores, and his standing suffered.
idiomatic: In Hanyang he had first won a solid name; later bribery and draining the border granaries cost him repute.

literal: Chieftains south of the Han and notables of Xiangyang sent secret letters inviting Shizun to bring Xiangyang over by inner surrender.
idiomatic: Tribal leaders south of the Han and men of standing in Xiangyang wrote secretly urging Shizun to receive Xiangyang from within.

literal: Shizun memorialized asking to respond; the court agreed and made him bearer of the staff, commander of Jingzhou and all forces south of the Han, General Who Pacifies the South, with added scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, other posts as before.
idiomatic: He asked leave to answer; the court assented, gave him the staff as commander of Jingzhou and the Han south, General Who Pacifies the South, and scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary.

literal: Inspector of Luo Yi Fansheng and Champion General Cui Mo, governor of Luyang, were sent as separate commanders with twenty thousand foot and horse under Shizun's orders.
idiomatic: Yi Fansheng, inspector of Luo, and Cui Mo, Champion General and governor of Luyang, led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry as detached commanders under him.

literal: When the army reached the Han, Mo and the others all hesitated and would not cross.
idiomatic: At the Han River Mo and his fellows hung back and refused the crossing.

literal: Shizun was furious and pressed them with troops; Mo then crossed.
idiomatic: Shizun raged and threatened force; Mo at last crossed.

literal: But the inside plot leaked; the conspirators were killed by Xiao Yan's inspector of Yong, who walled the gates and held firm.
idiomatic: The inner plot was betrayed; Xiao Yan's inspector of Yong killed the agents, walled the city, and stood fast.

literal: Mo burned the walls and suburbs of Xiangyang and killed tens of thousands.
idiomatic: Mo torched Xiangyang's walls and suburbs and slaughtered tens of thousands.

literal: That night a great wind with rain and snow blew; Mo and the others withdrew, and one or two in ten of the soldiers froze to death.
idiomatic: A night of wind, rain, and snow followed; Mo withdrew, and a tenth or more of the army froze on the march.

literal: Shizun, Fansheng, and Mo were all dismissed from office.
idiomatic: Shizun, Fansheng, and Mo were all removed from their posts.

literal: Later he was made scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, General Who Pacifies the North, and regional inspector of Dingzhou; the people were at peace under him.
idiomatic: He was later scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, General Who Pacifies the North, and inspector of Dingzhou, where the people rested easy.

literal: In the first year of Xiaochang he died in the province.
idiomatic: He died in the province in Xiaochang year 1.

literal: Posthumously he was scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, General Who Pacifies the West, regional inspector of Yong, and Prince Kang.
idiomatic: Posthumously he was scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, General Who Pacifies the West, inspector of Yong, Prince Kang.

literal: His son Jingxian inherited.
idiomatic: Son Jingxian succeeded.

literal: He served as remonstrating grandee and scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, and headed the Directorate of Imperial Wardrobe.
idiomatic: He held posts as remonstrating grandee and scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary and headed the imperial wardrobe directorate.

literal: When Yuan Hao entered Luoyang, Emperor Xiaozhuang toured the north.
idiomatic: When Yuan Hao took Luoyang, Xiaozhuang marched north.

literal: Jingxian and his uncle Jun rose at the He Bridge; Hao killed them.
idiomatic: Jingxian and his uncle Jun raised the standard at the He Bridge and were slain by Hao.

literal: Posthumously he was attendant-in-ordinary, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Preceptor, and regional inspector of Dingzhou.
idiomatic: Posthumously he was attendant-in-ordinary, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand Preceptor, and inspector of Dingzhou.

literal: His son Xuanhong inherited.
idiomatic: Son Xuanhong succeeded.

literal: He served as remonstrating grandee and vice director of the Palace Library.
idiomatic: He was remonstrating grandee and vice director of the Palace Library.

literal: In the Wuding era he plotted rebellion with Yuan Jin and was executed; the state was abolished.
idiomatic: In Wuding he conspired with Yuan Jin, was executed, and the fief was extinguished.

literal: Shizun's younger brother Jun, styled Shiping.
idiomatic: Shizun's younger brother Jun, courtesy name Shiping.

literal: He rose through posts to direct-palace attendant-in-ordinary and General Who Subdues the Barbarians.
idiomatic: He advanced to direct-palace attendant-in-ordinary and General Who Subdues the Barbarians.

literal: For merit in raising the standard at the He Bridge he was made founding baron of Ankang with five hundred households, and made scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary and General Who Pacifies the East.
idiomatic: For the He Bridge rising he was founding baron of Ankang, five hundred households, scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, and General Who Pacifies the East.

literal: On his death he was posthumously made bearer of the staff and General Who Pacifies the East, regional inspector of Qingzhou.
idiomatic: At death he was posthumously bearer of the staff, General Who Pacifies the East, inspector of Qingzhou.

literal: In the time of the emperor who departed he was again posthumously made Grand General of Agile Cavalry with opening-office equal-to-three-division and regional inspector of Ji.
idiomatic: Under the departing emperor he was again posthumously Grand General of Agile Cavalry with opening-office equal-to-three-division and inspector of Ji.

literal: Jun had six sons.
idiomatic: Jun had six sons.

literal: The eldest, Xinzhi, was rough and martial; even as a boy he had great strength.
idiomatic: Eldest son Xinzhi was coarse and warlike, strong from childhood.

literal: He began office as army adjutant of the Pingbei headquarters in Dingzhou and was gradually promoted to right army lieutenant in the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He entered service as adjutant in the Pingbei command at Dingzhou and rose to right army lieutenant in the Masters of Writing.

literal: For merit in the rising at the He ford he was granted the marquisate of Dong'a.
idiomatic: For the He ford rising he was made Marquis of Dong'a.

literal: When Emperor Xiaozhuang first plotted against Erzhu Rong and Yuan Tianmu, Xinzhi sent a secret memorial; on the day of action he begged to stand by and personally behead the two men.
idiomatic: When Xiaozhuang first plotted against Erzhu Rong and Yuan Tianmu, Xinzhi wrote in secret; on the day itself he asked to stand guard and cut down both men with his own hand.
